blocks.text: But the philosophers report a good many notable things about the nature of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab. That its penis is forked, as we said, Damir teaches in these words: للضب نكران وللانثي فرجان كما للورل وللحردون [li-l-ḍabb nakrān wa-li-l-unthā farjān kamā li-l-waral wa-li-l-ḥardūn] The male dhab has two penises, and its female two vulvas, like the guaril and the chardaun. And Alcamus: للنزك نكر الضب والورل ولهم نزكان [li-l-nazk nakr al-ḍabb wa-l-waral wa-lahum nazkān] Nazach is the penis of the dhab and of the guaril, which have a double one (the lexicographers, not understanding these words, twisted them to another sense). Accordingly the priest Abuchanipha writes that the penis of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان [ka-lisān al-ḥayya aṣl wāḥid lahu farʿān] like the tongue of a serpent, which, though born from one root, is nevertheless forked. It has a remarkably knotty tail, whence the proverb in Damir, اعقد من ذنب الضب [aʿqad min dhanab al-ḍabb] Knottier than the tail of the dhab. For they say there are حد وعشرون عقدة [ḥd wa-ʿishrūn ʿuqda] 21 knots in it, whereas the scorpion's tail, which is itself very knotty, has at most seven knots [?] joints. It is added that the same animal [?] has continuous [teeth], which therefore never fall out. [?] يقال ان اسنانه قطعة واحدة [yuqāl anna asnānahu qiṭʿa wāḥida]: [?] its teeth cohere into one. Alcamus: لا اتيك سن الحسل اي ابدا لان سنه لا تسقط [lā ātīka sinn al-ḥisl ay abadan li-anna sinnahu lā tasquṭ] The tooth of the chisel (that is, of the young of the dhab) will not come to you: that is, it will never come to you, because its teeth do not fall out. Here is another similar proverb about the same animal in Damir! لا افعله حتي يرد الضب لان الضب لا يرد [lā afʿaluhu ḥattā yarida al-ḍabb li-anna al-ḍabb lā yarid] I will not do this until the dhab goes down to the water (that is, I will never do it), because the dhab never goes down to the water. For it does not drink at all, and so it rarely urinates. The same: الضب لا يشرب الما [al-ḍabb lā yashrab al-mā] The dhab abstains entirely from drinking water. And a little later: يقال انه يبول في كل اربعين يوما مرة [yuqāl annahu yabūl fī kull arbaʿīn yawman marra] It is said to urinate only once every forty days, or قطرة [qaṭra] one little [col. 1048] drop, as another copy has it. On its eyes, in the same place: الضب يخرج من [II, 467] حجره كليل البصر فيجلوه بالتحدق في الشمس [al-ḍabb yakhruj min juḥrihi kalīl al-baṣar fa-yajlūhu bi-l-taḥadduq fī al-shams] The dhab comes out of its hiding place with rather dim sight; but when its pupil has been cleansed against the sun, it sees more clearly. Epiphanius, in the Sampsaeans, asserts that the σαῦραν ἡλιακὴν [sauran hēliakēn], the solar lizard, recovers its sight in the same way when it begins to grow dim: Ἐκείνη, he says, ἀμβλυωπήσασα χρόνῳ ἀναβλέπει, διὰ ἡλιακῆς στροφάλιγγος ἐν φωλεῷ πρὸς ἀνατολὴν προσέχοντι ἑαυτὴν προσθλίψασα, καὶ νηστεύσασα πρὸς ἀνατολὴν κατανοοῦσα· [Ekeinē amblyōpēsasa chronō anablepei, dia hēliakēs strophalingos en phōleō pros anatolēn prosechonti heautēn prosthlipsasa, kai nēsteusasa pros anatolēn katanoousa] When it has dulled sight, it recovers it some time later by turning toward the sun, pressing itself into a den facing the east, and, fasting, looking toward the East. Again Damir on the dhab: ويتغذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبره الهوا وذلك عند الهرم وفنا الرطوبات ونقص الحرارت [wa-yataghadhdhā bi-l-nasīm wa-yaʿīsh bi-l-barh al-hawā wa-dhālika ʿind al-haram wa-fanā al-ruṭūbāt wa-naqṣ al-ḥarārāt] And it is nourished by breath and lives on cold air, and this until decrepit old age, and until the (radical) moisture is consumed and the heat fails. And below: وهو طويل العمر ومن هذه الجهة يناسب الحيات والافاعي [wa-huwa ṭawīl al-ʿumr wa-min hādhihi al-jiha yunāsib al-ḥayyāt wa-l-afāʿī] It is a long-lived animal, which it has in common with serpents and vipers. And Ibno-chalvia: يعيش سبع ماية فصاعدا [yaʿīsh sabʿ māya fa-ṣāʿidan] It lives seven hundred years and more. This I think was invented by those who say greater things about great matters. But it is also altogether false, and wrongly transferred here from the account of the chameleon, that it is said to be fed by its own breath and to live on cold air. For it is an almost παμφάγον [pamphagon] animal, feeding chiefly on roots and fruits. Hence Alcamus, after writing that خبلة [khabla] chobla is the name for the roots of the vine and the fruits of thorny trees, adds: ضب خابل ياكلها [ḍabb khābil yaʾkuluhā] dhab chabil is a dhab that feeds on them. And the female, when stung by a scorpion, اكلت من حشيشة تسمي اذان الفار يزول عنها الم اللسع [akalat min ḥashīsha tusammā ādhān al-fār yazūl ʿanhā alam al-lasʿ] eats a herb called mouse-ear, and the pain of the sting abates. So it is in Alkazuinius. Moreover, on the authority of Damir himself (as will be said more fully below), the dhab returns to its vomit like a dog, and devours its own young. That it lives on air alone is therefore a mere fiction. It has this in common with the jarboa, or choerogryllius, that it chooses its hiding place in rocky and steep places. Alkazuinius: من كيسه انه لا يتخذ البيت الا في موضع صلب ليلا ينهدر عليه في حوافر الدواب ولما علم انه نساء لا يتخذ البيت الي عند الاكمته او صخرة عظيمة او شجرة ليستدل بها علي بيته اذا عاب ويتباعد عن [col. 1049] بيته [min kaysihi annahu lā yattakhidh al-bayt illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb laylā yanhadir ʿalayhi fī ḥawāfir al-dawābb wa-lammā ʿalima annahu nassāʾ lā yattakhidh al-bayt ilā ʿind al-akamatih aw ṣakhra ʿaẓīma aw shajara li-yastadill bihā ʿalā baytihi idhā ʿāb wa-yatabāʿad ʿan baytihi] It is part of its shrewdness that it does not take a home except in hard ground, lest, trampled by the hooves of beasts of burden, it collapse upon it. And since it knows itself to be very forgetful, it chooses it on a high hill or a lofty rock, or by a tree, which it may have as [II, 468] a marker when it is away from it or goes far off. Damir also: لا يتخذ حجره الا في كدية حجر خوفا من السيل والحافر ولذلك براثنه ناقصة كليلة لحفره بها في الاماكن الصلبة [lā yattakhidh juḥrahu illā fī kudyat ḥajar khawfan min al-sayl wa-l-ḥāfir wa-li-dhālika barāthinuhu nāqiṣa kalīla li-ḥafrihi bihā fī al-amākin al-ṣulba] Nor does it have a hiding place anywhere but in the hardest rocks, because it fears floods and diggers. And accordingly its claws are worn and blunt, since it digs stony places with them. Likewise: وفي طبعه النسيان وعدم الهداية وبه يضرب المثل في الحيرة ولذلك يحفر جحره عند الاكمة او صخرة ليلا يضل عنه اذا خرج لطلب والطعم [wa-fī ṭabʿihi al-nisyān wa-ʿadam al-hidāya wa-bihi yuḍrab al-mathal fī al-ḥayra wa-li-dhālika yaḥfir juḥrahu ʿind al-akama aw ṣakhra laylā yaḍill ʿanhu idhā kharaja li-ṭalab wa-l-ṭuʿm] Forgetfulness and ἀβλεψία [ablepsia] are natural to them. So its bewilderment has become proverbial. Accordingly it digs its den on a hill or in a rock, so as not to stray from it when it goes out to seek its food. The proverb Damir mentions is cited by him thus under the heading On Proverbs: اضل من الضب [aḍall min al-ḍabb] More apt to stray from the way than the dhab. Because the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is a wicked animal, whence it is called ضغطار [ḍghṭār] dhiphtar, as already observed, here is another proverb in use among the Arabs, which Alcamus taught me: اطعم اخاك كشية الضب حشة على المواسات [aṭʿim akhāka kushyat al-ḍabb ḥashsha ʿalā al-muwāsāt] He fed your brother the fat of the dhab, that is, he incited him to commit evil! As for breeding: اذا ارادت الضبة ان تخرج بيضها حفرت في الارض حفرة ورمت فيها البيض وطمته بالتراب وتعاهده كل يوم حتي يخرج وذلك في اربعين يوما [idhā arādat al-ḍabba an tukhrija bayḍahā ḥafarat fī al-arḍ ḥufra wa-ramat fīhā al-bayḍ wa-ṭammathu bi-l-turāb wa-taʿāhadathu kull yawm ḥattā yakhruj wa-dhālika fī arbaʿīn yawman] When the dhabba (that is, the female of the dhab) is about to lay her eggs, she digs a pit in the ground, into which she throws the eggs and covers them with dust, and visits them daily until they hatch, that is, until the fortieth day. So Damir, following Alkazuinius in part, whose words are: فاذا اراد ان يبيض حفر مثل ادحي النعام ويرمي فيها ثمانين بيضة ويدفنها [col. 1050] في التراب وبيضها مثل بيض الحمام ويدعها اربعين يوما ثم ياتي وحسول قد خرجت منها فيتعدون فياكل منها ما قدرت [fa-idhā arāda an yabīḍa ḥafara mithl udḥī al-naʿām wa-yarmī fīhā thamānīn bayḍa wa-yadfinuhā fī al-turāb wa-bayḍuhā mithl bayḍ al-ḥamām wa-yadaʿuhā arbaʿīn yawman thumma yaʾtī wa-ḥusūl qad kharajat minhā fa-yataʿaddawn fa-yaʾkul minhā mā qadarat] When it is about to lay, it digs something like an ostrich's nest, into which it throws eighty eggs, like pigeons' eggs, and buries them in the dust. When it returns to them after leaving them forty days, the young, coming out of them, run about. Of these it eats as many as it can. Indeed, as Damir says, يوصف العقوق لانه ياكل حسوله [yūṣaf al-ʿuqūq li-annahu yaʾkul ḥusūlahu] it is described as notable for cruelty, because it devours its own young. Hence the poet: [II, 469] اكلت بنيك كاكل الضب حتي تركت بنيك ليس لهم غذي [akalta banīka ka-akl al-ḍabb ḥattā tarakta banīka laysa lahum ghidhā]
